title: Animal Physiology / Comparative Physiology
short: How an individual animal's body works. Organs, hormones, metabolism, and the laboratory tools used to study them.
bigPicture: Physiology asks how animal bodies function: how they move, breathe, regulate temperature, process food, respond to stress, and hold internal conditions steady. The comparative branch studies that diversity deliberately, choosing the species best suited to a question rather than defaulting to standard laboratory animals. Practitioners describe it as much as a viewpoint as a discipline, which is why you will meet it as a course called animal physiology and as a professional section called comparative and evolutionary physiology.

terms.definition: Keeping internal conditions such as temperature, water balance, and blood chemistry stable despite changes outside the body.
The study of hormones and the glands producing them, and how they regulate body processes and behavior.
The rate at which an animal uses energy, often measured through oxygen consumption.
How an animal controls its body temperature, by behavior, physiology, or both.
The research strategy of choosing whichever species is best suited to the question, rather than defaulting to a standard laboratory animal.
Physiology studied in environmental context, asking how physiological limits shape where and how an animal can live.

focus.title: Systems and mechanisms
focus.description: How circulation, respiration, digestion, excretion, muscle, and nervous systems work, and how they are coordinated. This is the mechanistic core that clinical and applied animal fields build on.
focus.source: American Physiological Society (APS): Comparative & Evolutionary Physiology Section

focus.title: Regulation and homeostasis
focus.description: How animals hold internal conditions stable against changing external ones, including thermoregulation, water and salt balance, and endocrine control.
focus.source: American Physiological Society (APS): Comparative & Evolutionary Physiology Section

focus.title: Comparison across species
focus.description: Comparing physiological responses across many species to separate general principles from specific adaptations, and to understand how some animals tolerate conditions others cannot.
focus.source: American Physiological Society (APS): Lessons from Comparative and Evolutionary Physiology

focus.title: Physiology in ecological context
focus.description: Extending mechanism into the environment: how physiological limits shape where animals can live, how they respond to stress, heat, or scarcity, and what that means under environmental change.
focus.source: American Physiological Society (APS): Lessons from Comparative and Evolutionary Physiology

questions.question: How does this body system actually work in this animal?
questions.approach: By measuring function directly — respirometry, blood chemistry, hormone assays, telemetry — and then manipulating one variable at a time to see what changes.

questions.question: How does the animal keep internal conditions stable when external ones change?
questions.approach: By exposing animals to controlled changes in temperature, oxygen, or water availability and tracking the physiological response, including how fast it engages and how long it lasts.

questions.question: What does comparing species reveal that studying one species cannot?
questions.approach: By choosing species that face very different demands and testing the same system in each, following the principle of picking the animal best suited to the question.

questions.question: Where are this animal's physiological limits, and what happens near them?
questions.approach: By stepwise testing toward the limit under controlled conditions, measuring performance and recovery, with ethical review setting the boundaries of how far testing goes.

questions.question: How does physiology explain where a species can and cannot live?
questions.approach: By pairing laboratory measurements of tolerance with field data on where the animal actually occurs, then testing whether the physiological limit predicts the distribution.

questions.question: What is happening at the molecular level behind this response?
questions.approach: Through gene expression, protein, and metabolite work in tissue samples, connecting whole-animal responses to the mechanisms producing them.

responsibilities: Design and run controlled laboratory or field experiments on physiological function.
Collect and analyze physiological measurements, samples, and time-series data.
Maintain animals, equipment, and protocols to research and ethical standards.
Interpret mechanism in evolutionary or ecological terms and publish results.

variations.label: Two names, one field
variations.description: Animal physiology is the phrase you will meet as a course and textbook title. Comparative physiology is what the professional community calls itself, with sections and societies in many countries. Practitioners do not entirely agree it is a discipline rather than an approach, and the term is used somewhat differently by different researchers.
variations.source: American Physiological Society (APS): Lessons from Comparative and Evolutionary Physiology

variations.label: Where it sits
variations.description: Physiology courses live in biology, animal science, veterinary, neuroscience, and pre-health programs. Which department teaches it changes the emphasis considerably.

variations.label: Laboratory versus field
variations.description: Some work is controlled and instrument-heavy; some is done on free-living animals in their own environment, which is often treated as the harder standard.

variations.label: Adjacent paths
variations.description: This area feeds veterinary medicine, biomedical research, animal welfare science, and the physiological side of ecology.

realities: Much of the work is laboratory-based and instrument-heavy, with limited contact with animals in natural settings.
Research careers generally require graduate study; bachelor's-level roles are usually technician or research assistant positions.
Animal research is governed by institutional review and animal-use protocols.
The comparative label is not universally used the same way, so read course descriptions rather than titles.
careers: Research / laboratory manager — behavioral or biological science
